term: "GAN (Generative Adversarial Network)"
letter: "G"

## Simple explanation

A generative adversarial network (GAN) contains two neural networks: a
generator that creates samples and a discriminator that tries to
distinguish generated samples from real ones. They train in opposition,
with the goal of producing increasingly realistic samples.

## Technical explanation

The generator $G$ maps random noise $z$ to a sample $G(z)$. The
discriminator $D$ estimates whether an input is real or generated. In
the original formulation, the networks play a minimax game:

$$
\min_G \max_D
\mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_{\text{data}}}[\log D(x)]
+ \mathbb{E}_{z \sim p_z}[\log(1-D(G(z)))]
$$

Many variants change the objective or training procedure to improve
stability or sample quality.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

GANs helped establish adversarial training as a powerful generative
approach and have been used for image synthesis, translation, and data
generation. They can be difficult to train and evaluate, and generated
data may reproduce biases or artifacts.

## How it works

The discriminator learns from real examples and generated samples. The
generator receives feedback through the discriminator's response and
updates its parameters to produce samples that are harder to distinguish
from real data. Training alternates updates to the two networks.

## Practical example

A GAN trained on a curated collection of product images can learn to
generate novel-looking samples. Those outputs should be reviewed for
quality, memorization, and suitability before use.

## Common misconceptions

- The generator does not simply retrieve copies from the training set,
  although memorization can occur.
- A GAN is not guaranteed to converge to a stable or useful solution.
- Realistic-looking samples are not necessarily representative or
  factually valid.
